name: Sub specie aeternitatis (under the aspect of eternity)
plain_explanation: The wise person tries to see events not as located at a particular, emotionally charged moment in time but as part of the timeless, eternal order that God sees - so a disaster today should not disturb us more than an equally bad disaster in the distant past.
precise_definition: Spinoza's principle that reason, so far as human limitation allows, views things as God does: timelessly, so that whether an idea concerns something present, past, or future makes no difference to the mind operating under the dictate of reason.
why_it_mattered: It grounds Spinoza's rejection of hope and fear as irrational, since both depend on treating the future as uncertain rather than as fixed.
historical_origin: A direct consequence of Spinoza's determinism and his view that time itself is, in an important sense, unreal from God's perspective.
examples: Russell's counter-example: we are naturally more concerned about a disaster in our own time than one from the age of Genghis Khan, which Spinoza would call irrational.
objections: Russell argues this fails to distinguish future misfortunes we might still avert from past ones we cannot, though he notes Spinoza's determinism has a ready (if unconvincing) answer to this.

evolution.treatment: The wise person tries to see events not as located at a particular, emotionally charged moment in time but as part of the timeless, eternal order that God sees - so a disaster today should not disturb us more than an equally bad disaster in the distant past.
